passage: Dear Nazia, you asked why I've been so quiet. Papa wants me to skip the robotics camp in June and run our stationery shop during the wedding-season rush. At first I only felt a knot in my stomach, so I took a page and drew a line down the middle. Under Family Duty I wrote: Papa not working alone, being the child he can count on, the shop that paid for my school bag. Under My Ambition I wrote: building the sensor arm, proving a girl from our lane can do it, a certificate for engineering colleges. Looking at both, I saw they were about the same thing: being trusted and becoming someone. The knot got smaller. I still don't know what I'll tell him, but now I know what I'm choosing between. Write back? Arohi

qa.q: What did Arohi write under My Ambition?
qa.a: Building the sensor arm, proving a girl from our lane can do it, and a certificate for engineering colleges.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling before writing the two columns?
qa.a: A knot in the stomach: confused and torn, unable to separate the feelings until they were on paper.

qa.q: What could Arohi try next, and why?
qa.a: Ask Papa what the shop truly needs in June and suggest half-days, because facts might replace the either-or and let both needs be met.

qa.q: How might Papa see the request to skip the camp?
qa.a: Papa probably sees a busy shop and needs a dependable helper, and may not yet know what the camp means to Arohi.

grounding: A girl writes down what family duty and her own ambition each mean so the conflict is understood, not only felt.

passage:
You asked how I decided about the robotics camp, Chetan. It wasn't quick.

I'm Kavitha, and in April my parents asked me to skip the two-week camp in Chennai and help in our grocery shop, because Appa's helper had left. I felt torn in half. I'd waited a year for that camp.

For two days I just felt angry and guilty, in circles. Then my teacher said, "Beti, write down what each side actually means to you."

So I did. Duty: Amma looks so tired at closing time. The shop is how we pay my fees. If I say no, I'll feel selfish. Ambition: robotics is the first thing I've been really good at. The camp might help me get into an engineering course. If I skip it, I'll feel invisible.

Seeing both on one page, the feeling wasn't a fog anymore. It was two real things I cared about. Then I could talk to Appa.

qa.q: How long was the robotics camp?
How did Kavitha feel in the first two days after the request?
qa.a: Kavitha felt torn, angry and guilty, going around in circles.

qa.q: What could Kavitha do next, now that both sides are on paper?
qa.a: Kavitha could share the page with Appa and Amma and ask them to add their own worries, so they can look for a plan that respects both.

qa.q: How might Kavitha's parents see the situation?
qa.a: They may see the shop's real need and not realise how much the camp means, which is why Kavitha's written page could help them understand.

grounding: A spoken account of a girl asked to skip a robotics camp to help at the family shop, who writes down what family duty and her ambition each mean to her.

passage:
I'm Kishore, Jahnavi's younger brother. The week Appa asked her to skip the robotics workshop in Hyderabad to help at our hardware shop, she barely spoke at dinner.

Then one evening I saw her at the kitchen table with a sheet of paper folded down the middle. On the left she'd written "Family" and on the right "Me". I peeked when she went for water.

Under "Family": Appa's back pain, the Diwali rush, "they've never asked before". Under "Me": "I'm good at this", "the workshop is only once a year", "if I never go, I'll resent it".

She sat there a long time, crossing out and adding. I don't know exactly what she felt. But when she folded the paper, she didn't look as stormy. She took it to Appa's room and knocked.

I could hear them talking for a long time. Nobody raised their voice.

qa.q: What two headings did Jahnavi write on the paper?
qa.a: "Family" on the left and "Me" on the right.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi have been feeling when she barely spoke at dinner?
qa.a: She was probably torn and upset, caught between wanting to help the family and wanting the workshop.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi and Appa try after their talk?
qa.a: They could look for middle options, like part-time help at the shop or a cousin covering some days, so both needs are partly met.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi's evening look to Kishore?
qa.a: To Kishore it looked like a stormy silence turning into calm, careful thinking on paper, though Kishore can't be sure exactly what Jahnavi felt.

grounding: An observer describes a girl asked to skip a robotics workshop for the family shop writing down what family duty and her own ambition each mean to her.
